clue.text: Jester, one about to appear in royal house

indicators.note: to appear in a house is to be placed inside it, so these letters go into the house's name

parts.note: York is an English royal house, as in the Yorkist kings
one is the Roman numeral I
C is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A court fool, with something about to happen, turns up at a royal residence.
explanation.walkthrough: IC goes inside YORK. The jester is the one whose skull Hamlet holds: 'Alas, poor ...'
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet this character was the late court fool of the Danish king.

clue.text: Misguided aeroplane losing way in comic entertainment?

indicators.note: misguided suggests going astray, so the letters left are put into a new order
losing tells us the plane word drops a run of its letters

parts.note: a lane is a way or narrow road

explanation.surface: A badly directed plane goes off course in a comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' takes LANE from AEROPLANE, leaving AEROP; 'Misguided' rearranges those five letters. The question mark is there because only some of these stage works are comic.
explanation.definitionFit: Comic and light versions of this sung stage work are a recognised genre of entertainment.

clue.text: So is butter sincerely recommended?

parts.note: imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, and laying the butter on thick means flattering; so flattery, sincerely meant, is copying

explanation.surface: A doubtful question about whether a spread is honestly endorsed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter' is the verb to flatter. The proverb says imitation is the sincerest flattery, so the most sincere buttering-up is done by copying.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb makes copying the sincerest flattery, so such buttering is copycat behaviour.

clue.text: Could he have taken a risk, ill-advised, about English?

definitions.text: Could he have taken a risk, ill-advised, about English?

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the abbreviation
an ill-advised plan is badly arranged, so the letters of the two words before are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question whether some man gambled foolishly regarding England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ill-advised' rearranges A RISK to KAISR, and 'about' puts it round E. The whole clue doubles as a description: Wilhelm II took an ill-judged gamble against England.
explanation.definitionFit: The German emperor took a reckless gamble in the war against Britain, so the whole clue describes him.

clue.text: I'll miss gin, perhaps. almost none in diluted drink

indicators.note: the clue speaks for the letter itself: I will be missing from the drink word

parts.note: gin is an example of a spirit

indicators.note: almost means the word stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: zero means none

explanation.surface: Someone will forgo gin and take a watered-down drink with hardly anything in it.
explanation.walkthrough: SPIRIT loses one I to give SPRIT, and ZERO loses its last letter to give ZER. 'perhaps' marks gin as just one example of a spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: It is white wine mixed with soda water, a wine drink thinned with fizz.

clue.text: Obviously lacking instruction

parts.note: something so clear that it needs no telling, plainly without need of any guidance

explanation.definitionFit: Something so clear it needs no further account obviously does without instructions.

clue.text: Infection's grown nasty inside raised edge

indicators.note: inside means the jumbled letters go within the edge word

parts.note: a rim is a raised edge, as round a plate

indicators.note: nasty suggests something turned bad, so the letters of the word before are jumbled

explanation.surface: An infection has turned unpleasant beneath a lip of skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nasty' rearranges GROWN to NGWOR. 'Infection's' is the definition plus 'is' as a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a contagious fungal skin disease forming circular patches, so a kind of infection.

clue.text: Hair given very French style at first

parts.note: tres is the French word for very

indicators.note: at first asks for only the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Hair arranged in a very French way from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: TRES is French for 'very'; S is the first letter of 'style'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a long lock of hair, a poetic word for tresses.

clue.text: Disappear, having fallen out over a tape'

indicators.note: things that have fallen out are spilled and disordered, so these letters are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the stray mark being a printing blemish

explanation.surface: Someone vanishes after a quarrel about a recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having fallen out' rearranges OVER A TAPE. 'Fallen out' looks like a quarrel; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquid that turns to vapour vanishes, so the word also means to vanish.

clue.text: Fleming's agent used to keep physically fit

definitions.text: Fleming's agent used to keep physically fit

parts.words: Fleming's agent used to keep physically fit
parts.note: Ian Fleming's agent was a fit spy, but Alexander Fleming discovered an antibiotic agent that keeps people well

explanation.surface: A novelist's secret agent trains to stay in shape.
explanation.walkthrough: The reader thinks of Ian Fleming's James Bond; the agent is a drug, found by Alexander Fleming, and 'physically fit' means free of disease.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Fleming discovered this mould-derived antibiotic in 1928, a medical agent against infection.

clue.text: Rebecca's son' returned from exploit, penning article

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, so the article goes inside
returned means the word for exploit is read backwards

parts.note: to exploit something is to use it
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A biblical mother's son comes back from an adventure, writing an essay.
explanation.walkthrough: USE turned round is ESU, and A goes inside it. 'Exploit' looks like a noun for a deed; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Rebecca bore the twins Jacob and this hairy elder brother.

clue.text: Oriental's pranks catching Northern European

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Oriental's pranks catching Northern European (8)': JAPES around N plus E gives no JAPANESE; the wordplay needs an 'a' (JAP(A N)ES + E) that the OCR text lacks, and a search found no other printing

clue.text: Some of the crew is dominant — result of experience?

indicators.note: Some of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Part of the ship's crew holds sway, and this is what experience brings.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'creW IS DOMinant'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sound judgement is what years of living teach, so it comes from experience.

clue.text: Bond reported in from part of Asia

indicators.note: reported means the word is heard spoken, so its sound counts, not its spelling

parts.note: a tie is a bond, something that binds

explanation.surface: James Bond is said to be in an Asian country.
explanation.walkthrough: TIE, said aloud, sounds like the word for someone or something from Thailand. Capital-B 'Bond' suggests 007; it is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: It describes something belonging to Thailand, a country in south-east Asia.

clue.text: Asking about second person's health

parts.note: a greeting that enquires after the wellbeing of the one addressed, the grammatical second person

explanation.definitionFit: The common greeting enquires after the listener's wellbeing, and grammar calls the listener the second person.

clue.text: Time in the capital with an ardent supporter

indicators.note: in places the time letter inside the city name

parts.note: Paris is the capital of France
taken as written

explanation.surface: Spending time in the French capital with a keen fan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The capital' with no country named is taken as Paris here; the T for time sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A strongly committed follower of a cause or party is a partisan, an ardent adherent.

clue.text: Almost call in popular opinion for face-to face meeting?

parts.note: in means popular or fashionable

indicators.note: almost means the word stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: to term something is to call it by a name
a view is an opinion

explanation.surface: Nearly telephoning to get the public's view on meeting in person.
explanation.walkthrough: TERM loses its last letter to give TER. 'Call in' looks like a phone call; 'call' is the verb to name.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal conversation where questions are put in person, as for a job, is a face-to-face meeting.

clue.text: Rascal observed keeping friend quiet

indicators.note: keeping means the seen word holds the next letters inside it

parts.note: seen means observed
a pal is a friend
p is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A rogue is spotted keeping a mate silent.
explanation.walkthrough: P for quiet comes from music, where p (piano) marks a soft passage. The answer is an Irish word, rarely met outside crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an Irish word for a worthless fellow or scamp, so a rascal.

clue.text: What char may do, linking up with other char in a plant

indicators.note: the two words join so that a letter of the second crosses into the first

parts.note: a char, or charwoman, is a cleaner, who may sweep
char is also slang for tea

explanation.surface: A cleaner's duty, joined by a cup of tea, turns into a garden flower.
explanation.walkthrough: SWEEP and TEA join as SWEEPTEA, and the T moves into the first word to make SWEET PEA. 'Char' means both a cleaner and tea.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a climbing garden flower of the pea family, grown for its scented blooms.

clue.text: Get filled up, where drivers start to join motorway

parts.note: golfers hit drivers from the tee at the start of each hole
M marks a British motorway, as in M1

explanation.surface: A golf course fills up where players tee off near the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: Drivers here are golf clubs, not motorists; a TEE is where a golf hole starts. 'to join' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To swarm or be full to overflowing, as a place teeming with people, is to be filled up.

clue.text: Strike about to become isolated

indicators.note: about means the hit word goes round the next word

parts.note: to cuff is to strike with the hand
taken as written

explanation.surface: A walkout is about to leave the workers stranded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' suggests industrial action; it is a blow with the hand. 'become' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A village cut off by snow is isolated, separated from contact with others.

clue.text: In conversation, show resentment of a wedding

indicators.note: in conversation means the word is heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: to bridle is to show resentment or anger

explanation.surface: Someone talks bitterly about a marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: BRIDLE, to bristle with offence, sounds the same as the adjective for a wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: It means belonging to a bride or marriage ceremony, as in a bridal gown.

clue.text: Time to encapsulate Catholic's proud character in writing

indicators.note: to encapsulate means to enclose, so the time word holds the next letters

parts.note: a day is a period of time
RC stands for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: A period that holds a Catholic's arrogant figure in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The proud character is the hero of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, famous for his pride.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's hero in Pride and Prejudice is the haughty Mr Fitzwilliam of that name.

clue.text: Tank designed for Siamese fight ers?

definitions.text: Tank designed for Siamese fight ers?

parts.words: Tank designed for Siamese fight ers?
parts.note: Siamese fighting fish, or bettas, are kept in a glass water tank, not a military one

explanation.surface: A military tank is built for Thai soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tank' and 'fighters' suggest warfare; the fighters are fish and the tank holds water.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass water tank for keeping fish is what a betta, the Siamese fighting fish, lives in.

clue.text: Person with 12 supporting University's custom

indicators.note: in a down answer the supporting piece sits below the university letter

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university
12 across is the answer about the result of experience, and a person with it is a sage

explanation.surface: A wise person backs the university's tradition.
explanation.walkthrough: SAGE sits under U. The cross-reference points to 12 across, so the person with it is a wise one.
explanation.definitionFit: Habitual practice or established custom is usage, as in common usage.

clue.text: Mix red and yellow at first? I might

definitions.text: Mix red and yellow at first? I might

indicators.note: mix means the letters are stirred together into a new order
at first asks for only the opening letter of the colour word

explanation.surface: Someone who blends red and yellow paint says this is their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mix' rearranges RED plus Y, the first letter of 'yellow'. The whole clue is the speaker describing their trade.
explanation.definitionFit: One who colours cloth might well blend red and yellow to get orange.

clue.text: Italian writer using reason concerning the environment

parts.note: Umberto Eco was an Italian novelist and scholar
logical means using reason

explanation.surface: An Italian author argues rationally about green issues.
explanation.walkthrough: Umberto ECO wrote The Name of the Rose.
explanation.definitionFit: It relates to living things and their surroundings, so it concerns the natural world.

clue.text: What's needed to keep one's head above water?

definitions.text: What's needed to keep one's head above water?

parts.words: What's needed to keep one's head above water?
parts.note: the idiom about surviving money trouble, read literally as staying afloat

explanation.definitionFit: The upward force a liquid exerts lets a swimmer float, staying afloat literally.

clue.text: Law broken in other-worldly Hants town

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the uncanny word

parts.note: fey means other-worldly or fairy-like

indicators.note: broken means the letters of the word before are smashed and rearranged

explanation.surface: Justice is undermined in a strange town in Hampshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges LAW to AWL. Hants is short for Hampshire, a county in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a village and oil-refinery town on Southampton Water in Hampshire.
